title: Why Texas Toll Roads Stay Tolled: Where the Money Goes After Construction
subtitle: Where the money goes after construction, using audited system records, debt covenants, Texas statutes, and current concession terms.
evidenceBoundary: This article compares material Texas systems rather than claiming a statewide toll-revenue denominator. Fiscal years and accounting bases differ. Sponsor-reported concession metrics are not public-authority accounts. Four unresolved evidence items remain disclosed, and unavailable categories are not converted to zero or estimates.
htmlBody:
Build the road, collect tolls, repay the road, remove the toll. That is the model many drivers carry in their heads. It assumes one project, one construction bill, one loan, and a clean ending. The major Texas systems examined here pool roads, refinance debt, hold reserves, fund later capital work, transfer legally available cash, or operate under concession contracts whose terms last for decades.

SH 288 shows the break most clearly. Texas already held public title to the corridor, yet paid $1,731,730,721, less permitted adjustments, to terminate the private concession in 2024. Control transitioned to the public structure and tolling continued. The transaction changed contractual revenue rights and financing; it did not erase the state's legal power to charge.

01 / Evidence

“Paid off” is five different questions

A construction-cost calculation, a road's debt balance, a system's debt, a public body's tolling power, and a concessionaire's revenue rights are not interchangeable. A road can satisfy one test and remain tolled because another layer is still active.

The first test is historical economics. The other four determine whether the current revenue stream remains pledged, legally authorized, or contractually assigned.

02 / Evidence

The only clean $100 comparison in the current records

There is no single statewide Texas toll-dollar ledger. NTTA closes its year on December 31. Harris County, TxDOT, CTRMA, and Fort Bend use different periods and structures. Some entities disclose accrual expenses but not a complete current-year cash waterfall. Others include investment and non-toll revenue in the pledged denominator.

The normalized chart therefore contains only the Central Texas Turnpike System and Grand Parkway. Both rows come from the same TxDOT FY2025 report, use the same operating-revenue denominator, and follow the same category schedule.

For CTTS, each $100 of FY2025 operating revenue supported $30.17 of operating expense, $19.29 of repairs and maintenance, $47.49 of debt service, and $3.05 of required reserve. For Grand Parkway, the corresponding figures were $15.03, $4.82, $44.59, and $35.56.

03 / Evidence

Harris County shows why a toll-dollar stack can fail

HCTRA's FY2025 statements provide a useful cash-flow case, but not a closed allocation of one current toll dollar. The accounting view begins with $1.0276 billion of toll revenue and $542.7 million of operating expense. That expense includes $115.5 million of depreciation and amortization, which allocates earlier capital cost rather than recording a current cash payment.

The cash-flow statement reports $995.7 million received from customers, $404.8 million paid to employees and suppliers, $242.0 million of principal and interest, $315.3 million of capital purchases, and a $398.6 million transfer to Harris County's thoroughfare and mobility program.

The four selected uses total $1.3607 billion, or $132.42 per $100 of reported toll revenue. That does not mean HCTRA spent the same dollar twice. Beginning cash and investments, investment earnings, borrowing, and other sources also funded the year.

The $398.6 million line is a public transfer recorded in audited statements. It is not a private dividend. The financial statement alone also does not prove that the same amount could have reduced toll rates immediately; debt covenants, reserves, capital plans, and public approvals remain relevant.

04 / Evidence

Major public systems compared

The comparison below preserves each reporting entity's fiscal year and basis. A blank or unavailable field is not zero. It marks a category that the current records do not support on a comparable basis.

05 / Evidence

Recovering construction cost does not retire every claim

A project-cost recovery calculation asks whether cumulative net cash collected from drivers has exceeded the original design and construction cost. The answer changes with the definition of cost: right-of-way, capitalized interest, grants, financing fees, electronic collection, later widening, and rehabilitation may or may not be included.

Authorities generally do not maintain a legally controlling meter that applies each future toll receipt against one historical construction invoice. Even a careful historical answer does not usually cancel a toll.

A road may have no identifiable standalone bond remaining while its revenue supports a pooled system. Refunding bonds can replace prior debt to alter rates, maturities, or creditor terms. That is a financing change, not a second construction project.

06 / Evidence

NTTA: the toll belongs to a pooled Trust

NTTA's FY2025 audited report recorded $1.253 billion of net toll revenue, $1.105 billion of net revenue available for debt service, $675.7 million of audited debt service, 1.64 times coverage, and $8.519 billion of long-term debt. The debt schedule extends to 2052.

Those figures describe a Trust, not one road. Pledged revenue supports system operations and required debt payments before later uses. Coverage tests require revenue above bare debt service. Additional borrowing, reserve releases, and subordinate obligations remain governed by the Trust Agreement.

The December 2025 monthly report shows $1.3575 billion of gross Trust revenue, $252.7 million of net operating expense, and $666.9 million of preliminary cash debt service. The arithmetic remainder is $437.9 million.

That $437.9 million is an algebraic remainder in this comparison. The schedule does not trace it to one named fund. It is not labeled unrestricted cash, profit, a reserve deposit, or a capital allocation. Any later use remains subject to the pooled Trust.

NTTA also received about $630.5 million of refunding-bond proceeds during FY2025. Refunding changes creditor claims, maturities, and interest cost. It does not establish that a road was built twice or create an automatic toll-removal date.

07 / Evidence

HCTRA: toll-system cash can support county mobility work

The mobility transfer is the clearest public-system answer to where money can go after construction. Harris County used a material amount of toll-system cash for a broader transportation program. The audited record identifies the amount and recipient; it does not support calling the transfer an owner withdrawal.

At September 30, 2025, HCTRA reported $2.759 billion of bond principal with final maturities reaching 2054. Its revenue-bond covenant requires at least 1.25 times coverage under the governing calculation. Some obligations also have security or support features that differ from a pure standalone revenue bond.

The policy question remains open: more cash could remain in the toll system, support reserves and capital, fund county mobility work, or potentially affect rates. The accounting records the decision made. It does not decide which policy is preferable.

08 / Evidence

TxDOT's financed systems: excess enters the reserve structure

TxDOT's FY2025 toll report states that excess revenue for its debt-financed systems was deposited into project reserve accounts required by the bond documents. Under that schedule, CTTS and Grand Parkway reported no surplus available for an unrelated transfer.

Reserve and coverage requirements are part of the financing bargain. Investors lend against toll revenue because the project promises to maintain rates, coverage, and specified funds. A reserve can look like leftover money to a driver while remaining committed credit support.

The roads also keep absorbing capital after opening. TxDOT's FY2026-FY2030 planning records list rehabilitation, widening, interchange, technology, and safety work. Opening day is not the end of a road's capital life.

09 / Evidence

CTRMA and Fort Bend are included without invented comparability

CTRMA's FY2025 audit reported $276.4 million of toll revenue, about $2.448 billion of debt principal, and 2.28 times debt-service coverage. Its June 2025 statements provide more operating and debt detail, but the categories do not bridge cleanly to the audit without assumptions. CTRMA remains outside the normalized chart.

Fort Bend County has two separate toll authorities. FBCTRA reported $68.54 million of FY2025 toll revenue and $526.91 million of bond principal. Its $43.0 million of total expense includes noncash and financing-related items, so it is not used as cash O&M.

FBGPTRA publishes a separate FY2025 report and has its own financing structure. Combining the authorities or substituting countywide figures would make the analysis less accurate, not more complete.

10 / Evidence

Private concessions can distribute cash to shareholders

North Tarrant Express, LBJ Express, and NTE 35W are publicly owned corridors with long-term private concession rights. Their project companies finance and operate dynamically priced managed lanes, service project debt, and may distribute cash after satisfying contractual and financing tests.

Ferrovial's 2026 Factbook reported, at the 100 percent project-company level for the three Texas concessions, $935 million of FY2025 revenue, $776 million of adjusted EBITDA, and $553 million of project-company distributions. The same filing reported $318 million as Ferrovial's ownership-adjusted share of distributions.

Those are different denominators. The first set covers the complete project companies; the second is Ferrovial's share. Neither is the same as payments to TxDOT.

The filing separately reported $46.7 million of FY2025 payments to TxDOT: $26.4 million of NTE 35W revenue sharing, $8.1 million from NTE, a $6.6 million NTE 35W refinancing-gain payment, and $5.6 million of LBJ Wishbone revenue sharing.

The path is not toll booth to dividend. Debt service, distribution lockups, capital needs, maintenance standards, and public-agency sharing come first. The records nevertheless establish that a traffic-risk concession can distribute cash to private investors.

11 / Evidence

SH 130: bankruptcy changed the capital, not the toll right

Texas owns SH 130 Segments 5 and 6. SH 130 Concession Company holds the long-term operating and toll-revenue rights under the Facility Concession Agreement.

The original financing package totaled about $1.328 billion, including senior bank debt, a federal TIFIA loan, and private equity. The concession term extends to 2062.

The original project company filed for Chapter 11 protection in 2016 and emerged from restructuring in 2017. Debt and ownership economics changed. The road remained open and tolled.

A bankruptcy can write down or reorganize debt without terminating the concession. A new capital structure can replace the old one while the toll right survives.

Current public records identify the responsible concession entity and contract. They do not provide a clean ultimate-equity chain comparable to Ferrovial's public filing. This article leaves that ownership layer unresolved rather than carrying forward pre-bankruptcy names.

12 / Evidence

SH 288: the concession ended and the toll did not

The 2016 comprehensive development agreement gave Blueridge Transportation Group a long-term package of financing, construction, operation, maintenance, and toll-revenue rights. TxDOT retained public title.

In 2024, the Texas Transportation Commission used the agreement's termination-for-convenience mechanism. The stated payment was $1,731,730,721, less permitted adjustments. Control transitioned to the public structure on October 8, 2024.

Texas later reduced rates and retained the tolled managed-lane model. The private concession ended; public tolling authority did not.

The transaction was not proof that drivers still owed the original construction cost. Texas paid to end a private contract, assumed control of future revenue, and chose to keep that revenue inside a public project structure.

13 / Evidence

A Texas toll road can become free

The word never does not survive the statute book. Transportation Code §284.008 creates a default path for certain county toll projects. Subject to the statutory exception, a project becomes part of the state highway system and is maintained without tolls after project-revenue bonds and interest are paid, or sufficient money is placed in trust to pay them through maturity.

Subsection (d) lets a county request a Texas Transportation Commission order preventing that automatic transition. A February 25, 2016 Commission agenda records a Harris County request under the provision. The agenda proves the request existed; it does not identify the final order's complete scope. This article does not assign the exception to a named road without that order.

Other structures use different provisions. Section 366.407 addresses surplus revenue for regional tollway authorities. Section 370.174 addresses regional mobility authorities. Section 228.006 addresses surplus revenue from TxDOT toll projects. Bond documents and contracts may further constrain each statute.

  • Relevant debt and interest must be paid or legally defeased.
  • No pooled-system pledge may continue to claim the revenue.
  • Reserve, operating, and lifecycle-capital obligations must be addressed.
  • No concessionaire may retain a contractual toll right.
  • The responsible public body must have authority to remove the toll and choose to exercise it.
  • Another source must accept future operations and reconstruction costs.
14 / Evidence

Who can change or remove the toll

The decision-maker follows the legal structure. NTTA rates run through the NTTA board and Trust covenants. HCTRA policy runs through Harris County government and bond documents. CTRMA's board acts under Chapter 370. CTTS, Grand Parkway, and SH 288 sit under the Texas Transportation Commission and related public financing entities.

A private concessionaire may price within the formula, caps, performance standards, and public controls in its contract. A campaign promise, press release, or historical statement about toll removal is not a covenant.

15 / Evidence

Method, evidence limits, and correction route

The analysis uses the latest audited fiscal year available by September 2, 2026, supplemented by bond disclosures, monthly reports, statutes, commission actions, and concession documents. Figures are not combined across systems without the fiscal year and accounting basis shown.

The accounting view keeps operating revenue, operating expense, depreciation, interest expense, and change in net position separate. The cash and claims view keeps customer receipts, operating payments, principal, cash interest, capital purchases, reserve movements, transfers, borrowing, and ending cash separate.

Four items remain on the fact-check register: the final Harris County §284.008(d) order and project list, the current ultimate-equity chain for SH 130 Concession Company, a complete CTRMA audit-to-monthly category bridge, and exact page-level FBGPTRA headline extraction.

None is filled with an estimate. Corrections should record the date, affected claim, old value, new value, source, and whether the conclusion changed.

16 / Evidence

The better questions to ask about any toll road

The statement that a road was built years ago cannot resolve its current financing or legal status. These seven questions can.

  • Which entity has the legal right to impose the toll today?
  • Is the revenue pledged road-by-road, project-by-project, or systemwide?
  • What debt, interest, reserve, and coverage requirements remain?
  • Can residual cash be transferred, and for what legally permitted purpose?
  • Does a private concession have a term, termination formula, or reversion date?
  • Which board, court, or commission could lower or remove the toll?
  • What source would pay future operations and reconstruction after toll removal?
Downloads / Reproducibility

Financial model and evidence files

The package exposes the calculations and the limits behind the article. The workbook keeps same-basis comparisons, multi-source cash activity, concession distributions, and legal authority in separate sheets.

  • XLSX FY2025 financial model Nine-sheet workbook separating same-basis system comparisons, HCTRA cash activity, NTTA Trust arithmetic, concession cash, legal authority, sources, and claim audit.
  • CSV System comparison Material public systems with fiscal year, revenue basis, debt, coverage, pledge scope, comparison status, and source.
  • CSV Claim ledger Ten high- and medium-risk claims with evidence, calculation limits, publication wording, and unresolved actions.
  • MD Methodology Scope, five-test framework, accounting rules, normalized-comparison rule, and open evidence items.
